summary: Raahul Singh and Vanč Levstik from Phaidra present the concept of "Semantic Blindness," a failure mode where general-purpose LLMs cannot maintain structural awareness of physical systems despite large context windows. The problem arises when connecting LLMs to mission-critical industrial infrastructure with hundreds of thousands of sensors and equipment nodes. User queries range from checking specific equipment ("is chiller 6 running hot?") to analyzing groups ("all GPUs in data hall 1"), but industry naming conventions vary wildly—from descriptive names to cryptic codes. At 1GW-scale factories with 400,000+ GPUs, naive approaches fail: direct context-loading saturates LLM windows, vector-embedding RAG fails because similar names produce near-identical embeddings with poor recall, and sharded parallel LLM calls produce hallucinations and silent drops. LLM repetition/frequency penalties shut down output when listing similarly-named items. Phaidra's key architectural insight is that physical infrastructure has a hierarchical tree structure—data centers, data halls, aisles, rows, racks, GPUs—where depth grows slowly but width grows extremely fast. Rather than scaling with instance count (exponential), the solution scales with tree depth (sub-linear). Four pillars support their design: (1) a linearizer that provides a summarized graph representation listing root-to-leaf paths, keeping context small regardless of system size; (2) using LLMs for planning (structured outputs describing scope and filters) rather than searching; (3) a deterministic back-end that pre-indexes subtrees and uses set operations to guarantee perfect recall; and (4) pattern-based search for vague queries, where the LLM generates search patterns executed server-side. The end-to-end pipeline—user query → planner LLM → deterministic resolver → result set—is a 2-3 step process rather than an open agentic loop. Production evaluation showed the old approach degraded from 80% correctness at 64 GPUs to 30% at 460,000 GPUs while consuming 116M tokens per validation pass at 1GW scale, whereas the new approach maintained 100% accuracy across 66 real production test cases with 390,000 tokens total (~300x reduction) and flat per-query cost of ~9,000 tokens regardless of system size. The talk closes by invoking Karpathy's software 1.0/3.0 framing: legacy software drifts from deterministic 1.0 toward prompted 3.0, but new AI-native systems should invert this—start at 3.0 to discover what's worth building, then mature toward 1.0 by moving structured, reproducible logic into deterministic code. The guiding heuristic: if you can write down the structure or rules, it's a 1.0 job. LLMs should retain hard judgment—parsing ambiguous requests, deciding where to look, and synthesizing human-readable answers—while everything that must be 100% reproducible (retrieval, set logic, counting, dedup across near-identical names) belongs in code. Every 1.0 function added becomes more reliable ground for the LLM to stand on.

sections.title: Introduction and Problem Statement
sections.summary: Speakers introduce themselves and Phaidra's mission: building AI agents for AI factories that let users query data center operations. User queries range from specific equipment status to group analysis. Industry naming conventions vary wildly. At small scale, LLMs can handle equipment names directly, but at 1GW scale (400,000+ GPUs plus supporting equipment), LLM context windows saturate. A product must work for all scenarios without failing silently; a demo only needs to work for one.

sections.title: Why Naive Approaches Fail
sections.summary: Vector embedding RAG fails because equipment names differ by as little as one character (Chiller 6 vs Chiller 7), producing near-identical embeddings with poor recall. LLM frequency penalties shut down output when listing many similar tokens. Naive sharding with parallel LLM calls produces hallucinations (phantom equipment) and silent drops, unacceptable for mission-critical systems. The solution must scale sub-linearly with increasing equipment count.

sections.title: Hierarchical Tree Structure and Four Architectural Insights
sections.summary: Physical infrastructure has a hierarchical tree structure (data center → data hall → aisle → row → rack → GPU) where depth grows slowly but width grows fast. Four insights: (1) Linearizer—a summarized graph listing root-to-leaf paths keeps context small regardless of system size; (2) LLMs are good for planning (structured outputs describing scope and filters) but not for searching; (3) A deterministic back-end pre-indexes subtrees and uses set operations for perfect recall; (4) For vague queries, LLMs generate search patterns executed server-side, keeping LLM cost constant.

sections.title: End-to-End Pipeline and Production Evaluation
sections.summary: The full pipeline is user query → planner LLM → deterministic resolver → result set, a 2-3 step process rather than an open agentic loop. Production testing showed the old approach degraded from 80% correctness at 64 GPUs to 30% at 460,000 GPUs, while the new approach maintained 100% accuracy across 66 real production test cases. Token cost dropped from 116M to 390,000 per validation pass (~300x reduction) with flat per-query cost of ~9,000 tokens regardless of system size. The talk closes with a reference to Karpathy's perspective.

sections.title: Software 1.0 vs 3.0: The Inversion Principle
sections.summary: The talk closes by invoking Karpathy's software 1.0/3.0 framing: 1.0 is deterministic code (predictable, exact, inflexible); 3.0 is behavior prompted from an LLM (flexible, smart, fuzzy). Legacy software drifts from 1.0 toward 3.0, but new AI-native systems should invert this—start at 3.0 to discover what's worth building, then mature toward 1.0 by moving structured, reproducible logic into deterministic code. The guiding heuristic: if you can write down the structure or rules, it's a 1.0 job. LLMs retain hard judgment—parsing ambiguous requests, deciding where to look, handling novel phrasing, and synthesizing human-readable answers—while everything requiring 100% reproducibility (retrieval, set logic, counting, dedup across near-identical names) belongs in code. Every 1.0 function added becomes more reliable ground for the LLM to stand on. Speakers close with contact information.
